name: Margin and Capital Value Adjustments
source: Gregory, J. (2015). The xVA Challenge, 3rd Edition

questions.question: How does MVA differ from FVA, and what specific cost does each capture?
questions.answer_short: FVA covers funding costs from undercollateralisation (imperfect variation margin), while MVA covers the cost of posting initial margin (IM) and other overcollateralisation requirements.
questions.answer_long: FVA generally deals with cases of undercollateralisation, where unsecured MTM creates funding costs or benefits — it is largely a result of imperfect variation margin posting. MVA, by contrast, is a separate adjustment that quantifies the cost of posting initial margin and any overcollateralisation such as liquidity buffers. The key distinction is that FVA relates to the time-value of funding unsecured exposures, while MVA relates to the cost of holding high-quality segregated collateral that earns below-market returns.
questions.why_it_matters: Conflating MVA and FVA leads to double-counting or mispricing. As IM requirements grow under bilateral collateral rules and clearing mandates, MVA has become an increasingly significant standalone cost that must be tracked separately from FVA.
common_traps: Assuming FVA already captures IM posting costs
Treating MVA as simply another form of FVA
Forgetting that IM is not remunerated at OIS and therefore has an explicit cost
questions.real_world_example: A bank entering a bilateral swap under BCBS-IOSCO rules must post IM that is fully segregated and earns only a low repo rate. This IM cost is MVA. Simultaneously, if the swap is slightly undercollateralised on variation margin due to settlement lags, that cost is FVA. Both must be priced.

questions.subtopic: Two regulatory drivers of MVA and KVA
questions.question: What are the two key post-crisis regulatory developments that make MVA and KVA increasingly important?
questions.answer_short: 1) Initial margin requirements under clearing mandates and bilateral collateral rules, and 2) significantly more punitive regulatory capital requirements under Basel III (CVA capital charge, leverage ratio).
questions.answer_long: Since the global financial crisis, two regulatory reforms have driven MVA and KVA into prominence. First, both the clearing mandate and bilateral collateral rules (effective September 2016) require significant initial margin posting by both parties. Second, Basel III dramatically increased capital requirements for counterparty risk, including the CVA capital charge and leverage ratio, making the cost of holding regulatory capital a material pricing component that banks can no longer implicitly absorb into hurdle rates.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding these regulatory drivers is essential for understanding why MVA and KVA emerged as distinct xVA components. Before these reforms, capital costs were implicit and IM requirements were small; post-reform, both are too large to ignore.
common_traps: Thinking only clearing-mandated transactions face IM costs — bilateral IM rules apply too
Assuming Basel II-era capital is still relevant
Underestimating the impact of the leverage ratio on KVA
questions.real_world_example: After Basel III, a major dealer bank found that the CVA capital charge alone added several basis points to the cost of long-dated uncollateralised derivatives, requiring explicit KVA pricing to remain competitive while meeting return-on-capital targets.

questions.question: What costs arising from central clearing does MVA capture, and why is the default fund contribution included?
questions.answer_short: MVA covers CCP initial margin, default fund contributions, and potentially rights of assessment. These are costly because they are held by the CCP at below-market (often below OIS) remuneration rates.
questions.answer_long: For centrally cleared transactions, MVA covers: (1) IM posted to the CCP to cover worst-case default scenarios; (2) default fund contributions, which are also costly since they are held at near risk-free rates. Rights of assessment (future contingent default fund contributions) are typically unfunded and capitalised, so they appear more naturally in KVA. The cost arises because posted IM and default fund contributions are not rehypothecated and earn returns no higher than risk-free, and often less.
questions.why_it_matters: Including default fund contributions in MVA ensures the total cost of clearing is captured. Excluding them understates the true cost of a clearing mandate, which is directly relevant to the CCP vs bilateral cost comparison.
common_traps: Ignoring default fund contributions and only considering IM
Assuming rights of assessment belong in MVA — they are typically KVA
Forgetting that CCP IM is remunerated at below-OIS rates, increasing the net cost
questions.real_world_example: SwapClear requires both IM and default fund contributions. A clearing member pricing an IRS must include both in MVA, since both tie up capital earning sub-OIS returns for the lifetime of the trade.

questions.question: Why is bilateral IM under the BCBS-IOSCO rules particularly costly, and what rule governs its treatment?
questions.answer_short: Bilateral IM must be fully segregated and generally cannot be rehypothecated, so it earns only low returns. This segregation cost makes bilateral IM more expensive than variation margin.
questions.answer_long: Under the BCBS-IOSCO bilateral collateral rules (effective from September 2016), both parties to non-cleared derivatives must post IM. This IM must be segregated and cannot be rehypothecated (with one narrow exception). Segregation means the IM sits in a custodian account earning near-risk-free or below-market returns, and the poster cannot use it to fund other activities. This creates a meaningful cost that grows with trade maturity and IM size, captured by MVA.
questions.why_it_matters: The rehypothecation prohibition is what makes bilateral IM significantly more expensive than variation margin. Understanding this is crucial for pricing bilateral derivatives under the new rules.
common_traps: Assuming bilateral IM can be rehypothecated like variation margin
Thinking only the paying side has a cost — the receiving side also faces segregation costs
Forgetting that the rule applies symmetrically to both parties
questions.real_world_example: Under BCBS-IOSCO rules, Bank A and Counterparty B must both post IM on their swap. Each IM amount sits segregated earning 0.1% while each party's funding cost is 2%, creating an ~190 bps net cost that must be recovered via MVA pricing.

questions.subtopic: Contingent IM and LCR liquidity buffers
questions.question: What is contingent IM posting in the context of MVA, and how do LCR requirements affect how it is priced?
questions.answer_short: Contingent IM posting is IM that becomes required upon a ratings downgrade trigger. LCR rules require banks to prefund a liquidity buffer for a three-notch downgrade scenario, making this contingent cost real and priceable via MVA.
questions.answer_long: Some collateral agreements include rating-based triggers requiring additional IM upon a ratings downgrade (e.g., a three-notch downgrade). Even without actually being downgraded, banks must hold liquidity buffers under the LCR to cover these potential outflows. This means the contingent IM cost is not truly contingent from a liquidity perspective — the buffer must be held now. Banks therefore include this in MVA. Interestingly, it may be cheaper for a bank to post a small voluntary IM upfront to have rating triggers removed, since the held assets must be high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) regardless.
questions.why_it_matters: Misunderstanding contingent IM can lead to severe liquidity crises — exactly what happened with AIG in 2008. Proper MVA pricing ensures the prefunding cost of downgrade triggers is captured upfront.
common_traps: Treating contingent IM as zero-cost because the trigger hasn't fired
Forgetting that LCR requires liquidity buffers even for un-triggered contingent obligations
Ignoring that a bank generally cannot benefit from receiving contingent IM triggers under prudent LCR assumptions
questions.real_world_example: A bank with a three-notch downgrade trigger in its CSA must hold HQLA equal to the potential IM outflow, even at current ratings. This buffer earns near-zero returns, creating an MVA charge that should be reflected in the derivative's price at inception.

questions.subtopic: Why IM is costly — segregation and remuneration
questions.question: Why is initial margin costly even when it is received? What happens if IM is rehypothecated?
questions.answer_short: Received IM is typically segregated, so the receiver must also bear segregation costs. If IM were rehypothecated, a higher return could be earned, but it would create additional counterparty risk (CVA exposure).
questions.answer_long: All components of IM posting (CCP, bilateral, contingent) are costly because the IM must be held in high-quality segregated assets that earn at most risk-free, and often below risk-free, returns. Even when IM is received, the segregation requirement (to protect the poster) means the receiver cannot freely use the assets, creating an implicit cost. If IM were rehypothecated (used to fund other activities), returns could be higher — but this would expose the original poster to the receiver's credit risk, creating CVA for the poster. The cost of this CVA would then need to be covered separately.
questions.why_it_matters: This explains why both posted and received IM contribute to MVA, and why rehypothecation prohibition is a central feature of the bilateral IM rules. It also shows the regulatory trade-off between safety (segregation) and efficiency (rehypothecation).
common_traps: Thinking only the poster pays MVA — the receiver's segregation cost also matters
Assuming rehypothecation is always better — it just trades MVA cost for CVA cost
Ignoring that most CCPs remunerate IM at below OIS rates
questions.real_world_example: A dealer receives $50M IM from a client but must hold it segregated at a custodian earning 0.05%. The dealer's own cost of funds is 1.5%, creating a 145 bps drag on that $50M — a cost that should be priced into the trade via MVA.

questions.question: What statistical methodology is typically used to calculate IM for OTC derivatives, and what are the confidence level and time horizon standards for bilateral vs CCP transactions?
questions.answer_short: Historical simulation VAR or expected shortfall (ES) is used. Bilateral IM uses 99% confidence level over a 10-day horizon; CCP IM (e.g., SwapClear) uses a 5-day horizon, often calibrated to historical stress periods.
questions.answer_long: IM for OTC derivatives is increasingly calculated using VAR or ES. The BCBS-IOSCO standard for bilateral IM requires a 99% confidence level with a 10-day time horizon calibrated to a stress period. SwapClear uses historical simulation with a 5-day time horizon calibrated to 10 years of data, with IM defined as the average of the worst six moves — equivalent to approximately 99.76% ES. Both approaches now commonly include stressed data to mitigate procyclicality (the tendency for IM to be low during calm periods).
questions.why_it_matters: Knowing the IM methodology directly determines the MVA magnitude. A 10-day bilateral IM is roughly twice as large as a 5-day CCP IM, all else equal, making bilateral MVA potentially significantly higher.
common_traps: Confusing bilateral (10-day) and CCP (5-day) time horizons
Forgetting that stressed data inclusion raises IM but makes it more predictable
Using risk-neutral instead of historical simulation for IM calculation
questions.real_world_example: SwapClear's 5-day IM methodology means a dealer clearing an IRS faces a smaller but more predictable IM than under bilateral rules. This difference directly impacts whether bilateral or cleared execution minimises MVA.

questions.question: Why does including a fixed stress period in the IM lookback period make MVA more predictable, even though it increases the IM level?
questions.answer_short: A fixed stress period anchors the 99th percentile to the stressed losses, making IM more stable through time. Without it, the rolling 3-year window makes IM highly sensitive to which days enter/leave the dataset.
questions.answer_long: With a pure 3-year rolling lookback, the 99th percentile move changes dramatically as significant historical events enter and exit the window. This creates procyclicality: when markets are calm, IM falls; when markets are stressed, IM spikes. Adding a fixed annual stress period ensures the 99th percentile is consistently defined by severe historical losses. This makes IM higher (more conservative) but much more stable and predictable — which is important for pricing MVA, since an unpredictable IM profile is harder and more expensive to hedge.
questions.why_it_matters: Procyclical IM creates systemic risk (IM calls during crises when liquidity is tight) and makes MVA pricing unreliable. Understanding the lookback methodology is essential for projecting IM profiles accurately.
common_traps: Thinking a shorter lookback always gives lower IM — it depends on what events are included
Ignoring that both bilateral and CCP standards now require stress inclusion
Assuming the projected IM equals the expected IM — Figure 16.4 shows the expected is significantly higher due to asymmetry
questions.real_world_example: Post-2008, regulators found that rolling 3-year lookback IM models had very low IM during 2005-2007 (pre-crisis calm), then spiked dramatically in 2008-2009. Including a fixed stress period would have avoided this cliff-edge behaviour.

questions.subtopic: Asymmetric IM profile and Expected IM
questions.question: Why is the expected IM (EIM) profile significantly higher than the projected IM profile, and what causes the asymmetry?
questions.answer_short: IM can only increase substantially (as market moves worsen the VAR), but cannot decrease proportionally (the stressed floor provides a lower bound). This asymmetry means the average of all scenarios (EIM) is well above the projected (deterministic forward) value.
questions.answer_long: The projected IM is a deterministic forecast using current forward rates. The actual IM under Monte Carlo simulation depends on realised market moves that affect the VAR calculation. Since IM is based on worst-case losses, it spikes when volatility increases but cannot fall below the level defined by the stress period. This asymmetry — IM can jump significantly upward but reductions are bounded — means the expected IM (average across simulations) is materially higher than the simple projected value. This is analogous to the EPE being higher than the projected exposure for a similar reason (see Chapter 10).
questions.why_it_matters: Using projected IM instead of EIM will systematically underestimate MVA. Since MVA is negative from the bank's perspective, this leads to overpricing (charging too little for the IM cost), eroding returns.
common_traps: Using projected IM as a proxy for EIM — the asymmetry makes this a poor approximation
Thinking the projected vs EIM gap is small — Figure 16.4 shows it can be substantial
Ignoring the potential for methodology changes to create further upside IM surprises
questions.real_world_example: A dealer prices an IM-based swap using projected IM. A subsequent methodology change at the CCP (switching from relative to absolute returns for IR) raises actual IM by 40%. The dealer is under-reserved, because EIM would have partially captured this tail event.

questions.subtopic: IM methodology change — relative vs absolute returns
questions.question: Why does switching from relative to absolute returns for interest rate IM calculations have a more conservative effect in a falling rate environment?
questions.answer_short: Relative returns scale historical moves by current rate levels, so low rates imply small absolute moves. Absolute returns treat historical moves as fixed basis-point shifts, leading to larger IM when current rates are low.
questions.answer_long: Suppose historical data includes a rate move from 3% to 3.3% (a 10% relative increase). Under relative returns, if current rates are 2%, this translates to a 0.2% shock (10% of 2%). Under absolute returns, it translates to a 0.3% shock (the raw basis point move). In a low-rate environment (e.g., post-QE), absolute returns give larger shocks and thus higher IM. This is precisely why CCPs switched to absolute returns — relative returns were generating unrealistically small IM at very low rate levels, creating undercollateralisation risk.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding this switch is directly relevant to MVA projections: any future transition back to relative returns or volatility regime changes can dramatically alter IM levels, affecting MVA. Methodology risk is an unpredictable component of IM.
common_traps: Assuming relative returns are always more conservative — they are less conservative in low-rate environments
Ignoring that such methodology changes are one of the three unpredictable IM drivers
Treating past IM history as representative of future IM when methodology has changed
questions.real_world_example: After the ECB pushed rates to negative, CCPs found that relative-return VAR models implied negligibly small rate shocks. Switching to absolute returns corrected this and raised IMs substantially, materially increasing MVA charges for rate products.

questions.question: Write out the MVA formula and explain each component, including why the funding cost term is (FC - sIM) rather than just FC.
questions.answer_short: MVA = −∑ EIM(tᵢ) × (FC(tᵢ) − sIM) × (tᵢ − tᵢ₋₁) × S(tᵢ). EIM is expected IM, FC is funding cost, sIM is IM remuneration rate (possibly below OIS), and S is survival probability. The net cost is FC minus what the IM earns.
questions.answer_long: The MVA formula sums over time steps: MVA = −∑ EIM(tᵢ) × (FC(tᵢ) − sIM) × Δt × S(tᵢ). EIM(tᵢ) is the discounted expected IM at time tᵢ. FC(tᵢ) is the funding cost for the bank to post IM. sIM is the return earned on posted IM (often below OIS on CCPs). The survival probability S(tᵢ) represents the joint probability that neither party has defaulted. The cost is negative because IM posting is a cash outflow with no direct return. The (FC − sIM) term ensures that if IM earns a rate equal to funding cost, MVA is zero — the net cost only arises when the IM remuneration is below the funding rate.
questions.why_it_matters: The formula is the foundation for MVA pricing. The sIM term is often overlooked: CCP IM remuneration below OIS increases (FC − sIM), making CCP MVA more expensive than it might appear.
common_traps: Ignoring the sIM remuneration term and using FC as the full cost
Using projected IM instead of EIM, underestimating MVA
Forgetting the survival probability adjustment — it makes MVA smaller for riskier counterparties
questions.real_world_example: A bank posts IM at 2% funding cost; the CCP remunerates at 0.5%. The net cost is 1.5% per unit of EIM. For a $100M EIM profile, this 1.5% annually is material and must be priced into each new trade via incremental MVA.

questions.question: What is cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) optionality in the context of IM, and how does it differ from variation margin?
questions.answer_short: IM can typically be posted in different currencies and security types, creating optionality to post the cheapest eligible asset. Variation margin is usually restricted to cash in the transaction currency, so has no CTD optionality.
questions.answer_long: Both bilateral and CCP IM rules typically permit posting in a range of currencies and security types (e.g., G10 government bonds, cash in different currencies). This creates a cheapest-to-deliver option: the poster can always choose to deliver the cheapest eligible asset. This optionality has value and reduces the effective cost of IM posting — it should be reflected in the funding cost term FC in the MVA formula. By contrast, variation margin is generally required in cash in the transaction currency, so no CTD optionality exists.
questions.why_it_matters: Ignoring CTD optionality overstates MVA, since in practice the bank will always deliver the cheapest eligible collateral. This option value can be significant when there are material cheapness differentials between eligible IM assets.
common_traps: Assuming IM must be posted in the same currency/form as variation margin
Ignoring the CTD option and computing MVA on the worst-case IM asset
Confusing CCP and bilateral CTD eligibility — they differ
questions.real_world_example: A dealer required to post IM to SwapClear can choose between USD cash (earning OIS) or German Bunds (earning a haircut-adjusted lower return but costing less to source). The CTD option means the dealer picks whichever is cheapest on any given day.

questions.question: Why must MVA be computed on an incremental basis, similar to incremental CVA, and why does this create computational challenges?
questions.answer_short: IM is calculated at the portfolio level (across asset classes), so a new trade changes the entire portfolio's IM non-linearly. Incremental MVA = portfolio MVA with trade minus portfolio MVA without trade, requiring two full portfolio calculations.
questions.answer_long: Under bilateral rules, IM is calculated across asset classes for the entire counterparty portfolio. Under CCP rules, IM is netted across transactions in the same asset class. Adding a new trade therefore affects the portfolio IM in a non-linear way (due to diversification and correlation effects). To price MVA for the new trade, one must compute the full portfolio MVA with and without the new trade and take the difference. This is computationally expensive, especially when IM itself requires Monte Carlo simulation, and when capital interactions (KVA) must also be assessed.
questions.why_it_matters: Failing to compute incremental MVA correctly can dramatically mis-price new trades. The CME-LCH basis example shows that different clearing venues have different portfolio compositions, leading to very different incremental MVA charges for the same trade.
common_traps: Computing standalone trade MVA and ignoring portfolio netting effects
Assuming incremental MVA is always negative — portfolio diversification can reduce MVA
Underestimating the computational burden of nested simulation for IM
questions.real_world_example: The CME-LCH basis: clearing a swap at CME vs LCH can have very different incremental MVA because existing portfolios at each CCP are directional. The same trade may reduce portfolio IM at one CCP while increasing it at the other.

questions.question: What is the nested simulation problem in MVA computation, and what approaches can address it?
questions.answer_short: Computing EIM requires simulating future IM at each scenario node, but IM itself requires a VAR simulation — creating a simulation within a simulation. Approaches include delta-gamma approximations and American Monte Carlo methods.
questions.answer_long: The MVA formula requires the expected IM at each future time step across many Monte Carlo scenarios. At each scenario node, computing the exact IM requires running another VAR simulation (inner simulation). This 'simulation within simulation' (nested Monte Carlo) is extremely computationally expensive. Two solutions are: (1) local approximations using delta and gamma (though Green and Kenyon note these may be too approximate for the extreme moves involved in VAR); and (2) American Monte Carlo (regression-based) methods that estimate future IM using basis functions of current state variables, avoiding the inner simulation.
questions.why_it_matters: The nested simulation problem is the main computational barrier to accurate MVA pricing. Banks that cannot solve this problem must use approximations that may systematically mis-price trades.
common_traps: Assuming delta-gamma approximation is always sufficient — it may fail for large moves at high confidence levels
Ignoring the nested simulation problem and using only projected (not expected) IM
Confusing the outer simulation (exposure paths) with the inner simulation (IM calculation)
questions.real_world_example: A bank pricing MVA on a 10-year swaption portfolio uses American Monte Carlo to regress future SIMM-based IM against current market state variables (rates, vols), avoiding the need to run a full SIMM calculation at each of 100,000 scenarios × 120 monthly time steps.

questions.question: Explain qualitatively why MVA for a 10-day, 99% bilateral IM is approximately equal to FCA for a 5-year swap, according to the approximation in Section 16.2.4.
questions.answer_short: MVA is lower than FCA due to the shorter time horizon (10 days vs multi-year), but higher because IM is at a 99% confidence level vs the expected (mean) cost in FCA. These two effects roughly cancel for 5-year swaps, giving MVA ≈ FCA.
questions.answer_long: The approximation in Equation 16.2 gives the ratio of MVA to FCA as proportional to 2 × √(τIM/T) × Φ⁻¹(α)/φ(0). The first term, √(τIM/T), reduces MVA relative to FCA because IM covers only a 10-day horizon (short), not the full multi-year portfolio lifetime. The second term, Φ⁻¹(α)/φ(0), increases MVA because IM is computed at a high confidence level (99%), whereas FCA uses the expected (mean) unsecured exposure. For a 5-year swap with 10-day IM at 99%, the numerical result is approximately 1.04, meaning MVA ≈ FCA. This implies that from a pure funding perspective, a 5-year swap is roughly cost-neutral between IM and FCA environments.
questions.why_it_matters: This comparison helps practitioners understand when IM posting is beneficial vs harmful compared to FCA. The chapter argues that for longer maturities, IM becomes more attractive by shortening the effective funding horizon.
common_traps: Assuming IM is always more expensive than FCA — the short time horizon partially offsets the high confidence level
Ignoring the CVA and capital benefits of IM when comparing total cost
Applying the approximation mechanically without checking the normal distribution assumptions
questions.real_world_example: Table 16.1: FCA = -0.0706, MVA (10-day, 99%) = -0.0688. The near-equality confirms the approximation and shows that IM posting is slightly beneficial for 5-year swaps when all costs are considered, because it also reduces CVA.

questions.subtopic: KVA rationale — historical vs explicit capital pricing
questions.question: How did banks historically price capital costs into derivative transactions, and why has this approach become insufficient under Basel III?
questions.answer_short: Banks historically used capital hurdle rates — requiring a transaction to meet a minimum return-on-capital threshold. Basel III's larger and more complex capital requirements made this implicit approach too imprecise, driving explicit KVA pricing.
questions.answer_long: Traditionally, banks priced capital implicitly by setting internal hurdle rates for return on capital. If a trade did not meet the hurdle, it was rejected. This approach did not properly price the lifetime cost of holding capital — it was a binary gate rather than a continuous measurement. With Basel III introducing the CVA capital charge, leverage ratio constraints, and much larger overall capital requirements, this implicit approach became too imprecise. KVA emerged to explicitly compute and charge the expected cost of regulatory capital over the full life of a transaction, similar to how CVA explicitly prices counterparty credit risk.
questions.why_it_matters: The shift from hurdle rates to KVA is analogous to the earlier shift from PFE limits to CVA. Understanding the rationale explains why KVA is not optional for banks trying to achieve proper risk-adjusted pricing under Basel III.
common_traps: Thinking hurdle rates and KVA are equivalent — KVA captures lifetime cost while hurdles are one-time gates
Assuming pre-Basel III capital pricing was adequate for modern regulation
Forgetting that KVA differences are cited as the biggest source of price divergence between dealers
questions.real_world_example: Figure 16.5 shows that different KVA treatment is the most commonly cited reason for price divergence among dealers in the Solum CVA survey 2015 — confirming that KVA is both material and not yet standardised.

questions.subtopic: Three forms of capital in KVA
questions.question: What are the three forms of regulatory capital that contribute to KVA, and which two does the chapter focus on?
questions.answer_short: The three forms are: (1) default risk capital charge (CCR capital), (2) CVA capital charge, and (3) market risk capital charge. The chapter focuses on the first two, as market risk capital on CVA hedges has been largely exempted in key jurisdictions.
questions.answer_long: KVA must capture all capital charges attributable to a derivative transaction. These are: (1) Default risk (CCR) capital charge — capitalising potential counterparty default; (2) CVA capital charge — capitalising MTM volatility from credit spread movements; (3) Market risk capital charge — arising because CVA hedges may appear as naked positions in market risk frameworks. The book focuses on charges (1) and (2) because charge (3) — while potentially significant — has been largely exempted for CVA hedges in the US, Canada, and is expected to follow in other regions. BCBS (2015) also proposes capital frameworks reducing charge (3).
questions.why_it_matters: Using all three charges could lead to significant double-counting. Understanding which charges are applicable is critical for KVA accuracy and for regulatory compliance.
common_traps: Including market risk capital on CVA hedges in jurisdictions that have exempted it
Treating the three charges as additive when they interact (e.g., hedging reduces CVA capital but may create market risk capital)
Ignoring that KVA on CCP exposures is generally small (usually excluded)
questions.real_world_example: A US dealer hedges CVA with CDS. The CDS hedge creates no market risk capital charge (exempted). The dealer uses only CCR + CVA capital charges in KVA, keeping the pricing consistent with the regulatory framework they operate under.

questions.question: Why does the expected capital under CEM significantly exceed the projected capital, while for SA-CCR and IMM the two are much closer?
questions.answer_short: CEM current exposure uses only positive MTM with no offset for negative MTM, so capital can only stay the same or increase as MTM moves. SA-CCR and IMM recognise negative MTM as risk-reducing, creating symmetric paths where expected ≈ projected.
questions.answer_long: Under CEM, the current exposure term is max(MTM, 0), so negative MTM values provide no capital reduction (see Section 8.2.1). The capital cannot decrease below the initial add-on level for an at-market trade. This one-sided behaviour means the expected capital (averaging over all scenarios) is well above the projected (deterministic forward) capital. For SA-CCR and IMM, negative MTM reduces the calculated exposure (though SA-CCR has a 5% floor), making capital paths approximately symmetric around the projected value. As a result, expected capital ≈ projected capital for these methods — a much more efficient and accurate representation.
questions.why_it_matters: For KVA purposes, using projected rather than expected capital under CEM can underestimate the true cost by almost 50% (Table 16.2). This asymmetry is one reason CEM performs poorly at the portfolio level.
common_traps: Assuming CEM expected capital ≈ projected capital — it can be almost double
Thinking SA-CCR and IMM always give lower KVA than CEM — they are lower expected, but Table 16.2 shows SA-CCR actual > CEM projected
Forgetting the 5% replacement cost floor in SA-CCR that limits the capital reduction benefit
questions.real_world_example: Table 16.2: For uncollateralised 7-year IRS, CEM projected KVA is -0.457 but actual (with MC simulation) is -0.881 — almost double. SA-CCR projected is -1.502, actual is -1.758 (much smaller gap). This asymmetry is the key CEM flaw.

questions.question: Write the KVA formula and explain each term, including the choices available for discounting the expected capital profile.
questions.answer_short: KVA = −∑ EC(tᵢ) × CC(tᵢ) × Δt × S(tᵢ). EC is expected capital, CC is cost of capital, Δt is the time step, and S is survival probability. Discounting can use cost of capital (traditional), risk-free rate, or no discounting.
questions.answer_long: The KVA formula is: KVA = −∑ EC(tᵢ) × CC(tᵢ) × (tᵢ − tᵢ₋₁) × S(tᵢ), where EC(tᵢ) is the discounted expected capital at time tᵢ, CC(tᵢ) is the cost of capital (the required return on equity, e.g., from CAPM or dividend policy — typically 10-12%), and S(tᵢ) is the joint survival probability. The EC is traditionally discounted by the cost of capital rate. Some practitioners discount at the risk-free rate or not at all, arguing that capital requirements are not present-valued in the same way. Banks may also escalate CC over time to reflect anticipated future regulatory tightening.
questions.why_it_matters: The choice of discount rate and cost of capital directly determines KVA magnitude. A 10% vs 15% cost of capital can change KVA by 50%, leading to significant price divergence between banks.
common_traps: Using the wrong discount rate for EC (using OIS when cost of capital is appropriate)
Treating CC as fixed when it may be time-varying
Forgetting that KVA is a portfolio-level calculation (CVA capital is not additive across netting sets)
questions.real_world_example: Two competing dealers quote different prices for the same IRS. Dealer A uses 10% cost of capital with OIS discounting of EC; Dealer B uses 15% cost of capital with cost-of-capital discounting. This is a primary reason for the price divergence in Figure 16.5.

questions.question: Why must KVA be calculated at the entire portfolio level simultaneously, and what computational challenge does this create for pricing new transactions?
questions.answer_short: CVA capital is a portfolio-level calculation in both standardised and advanced versions — it cannot be decomposed additively. Pricing a new trade requires computing portfolio KVA with and without the trade, creating an expensive incremental calculation.
questions.answer_long: The default risk capital charge is additive across netting sets, but the CVA capital charge is a portfolio-wide calculation under both the standardised and advanced approaches. This means the CVA capital for a new trade cannot be computed in isolation — it depends on the entire existing portfolio's credit spreads, maturities, and netting. To compute incremental KVA for a new trade, one must compute portfolio KVA with and without the trade and subtract. Under IMM, where capital itself requires Monte Carlo simulation, this nested portfolio-level computation is extremely expensive. Capital-reducing hedges must also be incorporated, adding further complexity.
questions.why_it_matters: This computational challenge explains why many banks approximate KVA (using projected rather than expected capital) and why KVA pricing is less standardised than CVA. It also explains why large banks with IMM approval can have very different KVA charges than banks using CEM.
common_traps: Treating KVA as additive across trades — only default risk capital is additive
Ignoring the impact of existing portfolio composition on new trade KVA
Forgetting to include capital-reducing hedges (single-name CDS) in the EC profile
questions.real_world_example: A bank with IMM approval finds that each new uncollateralised trade requires running a full portfolio exposure simulation to compute incremental CVA capital. This takes hours, making real-time KVA pricing during negotiations impossible without approximation.

questions.subtopic: KVA term structure for forward transactions
questions.question: Why does the capital profile for an FX forward project approximately flat through time, unlike an interest rate swap which decays to zero?
questions.answer_short: FX forwards have no periodic cashflows, so the exposure remains approximately flat (square-root-of-time EE shape) until maturity. IRS have periodic cashflows that gradually reduce the outstanding notional and thus the exposure.
questions.answer_long: For an interest rate swap, periodic coupon exchanges reduce the effective notional at risk, so the exposure (and capital) decays towards zero as maturity approaches. For an FX forward, there are no intermediate cashflows — the full notional is at risk until settlement at maturity. Under historical volatility (flat volatility term structure), the EE follows a square-root-of-time shape, which projects as approximately flat for moderate maturities. This means the capital profile is flat rather than amortising, producing a larger KVA for FX forwards relative to swaps of similar notional and maturity.
questions.why_it_matters: This term structure difference has material pricing implications. FX forward KVA can be much larger than expected if incorrectly modelled using a decaying profile. The flat capital profile also makes KVA for cross-currency swaps relatively large.
common_traps: Applying a linearly decaying capital profile to FX forwards — the profile is approximately flat
Ignoring that implied volatility can create an upward-sloping capital profile (Figure 16.8)
Assuming cross-currency swaps behave like IR swaps — they also have approximately flat profiles
questions.real_world_example: A 10-year USD/EUR FX forward has a flat capital profile, meaning the KVA is proportional to the full 10-year period. An equivalent 10-year IRS has amortising capital, giving a materially lower KVA.

questions.subtopic: Real-world vs risk-neutral calibration for KVA
questions.question: Why should KVA typically be calculated using real-world parameters rather than risk-neutral parameters, unlike CVA and FVA?
questions.answer_short: CVA and FVA are hedged and reflected in financial statements, requiring risk-neutral calibration. KVA is generally not hedged or marked-to-market — the actual regulatory capital required in the real world is what matters, pointing to real-world parameters.
questions.answer_long: CVA uses risk-neutral default probabilities because it represents the fair value of a hedge that can theoretically be put on at market prices. FVA similarly uses risk-neutral calibrations since it is reflected in pricing and accounting. KVA, by contrast, is generally not transfer-priced to an xVA desk, not hedged in the market, and not reflected in accounting statements. Therefore, what matters is the actual real-world capital required by regulators — which depends on real-world scenarios, not risk-neutral pricing distributions. Risk-neutral calibrations may produce different (often larger) capital profiles due to implied volatility being above historical, changing the KVA estimate.
questions.why_it_matters: The calibration choice can materially change the shape and level of the capital profile (as shown in Figure 16.8). Using risk-neutral when real-world is appropriate (or vice versa) creates systematic mispricing of KVA.
common_traps: Using risk-neutral parameters for KVA by analogy with CVA — KVA requires real-world
Assuming the two calibrations always agree — Figure 16.8 shows they can diverge materially
Forgetting that if a bank decides to hedge KVA in the future, risk-neutral parameters become more relevant
questions.real_world_example: Figure 16.8: Using implied vs historical volatility for a 10-year FX forward produces different shapes — implied volatility makes EE lower near term and higher long term. Under real-world (historical) calibration, the projected capital is flat; under risk-neutral, it grows over time, increasing KVA for long-dated trades.

questions.question: Why is KVA described as the most subjective xVA component, and what are four sources of regulatory uncertainty that affect KVA?
questions.answer_short: KVA is most subjective because future regulatory capital requirements are uncertain. Key uncertainties include: (1) capital methodology changes (CEM→SA-CCR→IMM), (2) leverage ratio finalisation, (3) CVA capital exemptions, and (4) capital relief from hedges.
questions.answer_long: Unlike CVA (driven by observable credit spreads) and FVA (driven by funding markets), KVA depends on future regulatory capital rules that are explicitly uncertain. The four main sources: (1) Capital methodology: banks may switch from CEM to SA-CCR or gain IMM approval, significantly changing capital levels. (2) Leverage ratio: set at 3% in Europe with US considering 4-6%; the final calibration (not until 2017) was unknown at time of writing. (3) CVA exemptions: European banks enjoyed CVA exemptions for many counterparties — future reversal is uncertain. (4) Hedge eligibility: whether single-name CDS hedges provide capital relief depends on future market liquidity and regulatory decisions.
questions.why_it_matters: The subjectivity of KVA is the primary reason it is cited as the largest source of dealer price divergence (Figure 16.5). Banks making different regulatory assumptions will price the same trade very differently.
common_traps: Treating KVA as an objective calculation like CVA
Ignoring the potential for regulatory changes to materially affect long-dated transactions
Using current methodology without considering likely future changes
questions.real_world_example: A bank pricing a 10-year swap in 2015 must make assumptions about: whether CVA exemptions will be removed (raises KVA by 5-10x for sovereign counterparties), whether IMM approval will be obtained (changes capital profile shape), and whether the leverage ratio will rise to 5% (raises KVA significantly). Each assumption can swing the price by basis points.

questions.question: How do counterparty behavioural assumptions affect KVA, and why might KVA be lower for a hedge fund client than a corporate?
questions.answer_short: Hedge funds frequently unwind transactions early, reducing actual capital held and thus KVA. Corporates hedging debt issuance typically hold transactions to maturity, resulting in higher KVA for the full life of the trade.
questions.answer_long: Because KVA uses real-world capital requirements, the actual behaviour of the counterparty matters. A hedge fund that typically unwinds positions within 2-3 years of inception creates a shorter effective capital horizon than the contractual maturity, reducing KVA. A corporate that entered the swap specifically to hedge a debt issuance will hold it to maturity (10+ years), leading to maximum KVA exposure. Banks therefore incorporate client-specific behavioural factors — based on past behaviour and business rationale — into their KVA calculations. This is another source of subjectivity.
questions.why_it_matters: Behavioural assumptions can materially reduce KVA for certain client types. Ignoring them means overpricing and potentially losing business to competitors who correctly account for early termination.
common_traps: Using contractual maturity for all counterparties when early termination is common for some
Applying hedge fund termination behaviour to corporate clients
Ignoring that early termination assumptions must be supported by documented evidence
questions.real_world_example: A bank prices a 10-year swap with a hedge fund client. The hedge fund has historically unwound similar positions in year 3 on average. Using a 3-year effective maturity for KVA rather than 10 years reduces KVA by ~60%, making the bank's price significantly more competitive.

questions.question: How does collateral posting affect KVA, and why is the gap between projected and actual KVA much smaller in the collateralised case for all methodologies?
questions.answer_short: Collateral reduces exposure, lowering EC and thus KVA. In the collateralised case, negative MTM is correctly recognised by all methods (since collateral is assumed held against positive MTM), making projected ≈ actual for all methodologies.
questions.answer_long: With collateral (a 10-day MPR assumed), the bank holds collateral equal to the positive MTM, significantly reducing the exposure remaining at risk. This reduces EC and hence KVA. More importantly, when collateral is correctly modelled, even CEM shows projected ≈ actual capital (Table 16.2: CEM collateralised projected = actual = -0.457), because the optionality of negative MTM providing no offset (the CEM flaw for uncollateralised trades) is removed — the collateral holder always realises the full MTM. For SA-CCR and IMM, collateralised KVA is further reduced relative to CEM due to better netting recognition.
questions.why_it_matters: This confirms the capital benefit of collateralisation under all methodologies, supporting the regulatory push for collateral posting. It also shows that for collateralised trades, projected KVA is a reasonable approximation, simplifying computation.
common_traps: Assuming collateral only helps with CVA and not KVA — it reduces both
Thinking CEM and SA-CCR always give similar results for collateralised trades — SA-CCR and IMM give lower KVA
Forgetting that the MPR (10 days) still creates residual capital in the collateralised case
questions.real_world_example: Table 16.2: Uncollateralised IMM actual KVA = -1.249; collateralised IMM actual = -0.367. Posting collateral reduces KVA by about 70%, confirming the strong capital benefit of full collateralisation.

questions.question: Why are KVA and MVA not mutually exclusive, and for what types of transactions does each dominate?
questions.answer_short: IM reduces capital (since it protects the bank against counterparty default), so receiving IM reduces KVA while increasing MVA. For uncollateralised transactions KVA dominates; for centrally cleared transactions MVA dominates.
questions.answer_long: IM can be seen as capital provided by the counterparty — received IM reduces the bank's exposure and therefore its capital requirements. This means increasing IM reduces KVA. However, posting IM increases MVA (the cost of the posted IM). The net effect depends on whether the KVA reduction from received IM outweighs the MVA increase. For uncollateralised transactions, KVA is clearly significant; for centrally cleared, MVA dominates (IM reduces capital to near zero). Under IMM methodology, there is actually an overall benefit to moderate bilateral IM because debt financing is cheaper than equity (capital). However, the law of diminishing returns means each additional unit of IM has decreasing KVA benefit.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the KVA-MVA trade-off is essential for determining optimal collateral strategies. The chapter suggests bilateral IM requirements are not justified purely by KVA reduction (it would imply regulatory arbitrage), but that the combined CVA+FVA+KVA impact may make higher IM beneficial.
common_traps: Treating KVA and MVA as entirely separate costs when they interact strongly
Assuming more IM is always better for total xVA — diminishing returns apply
Ignoring that CEM does not recognise IM in capital calculations at all
questions.real_world_example: Figure 16.9: As bilateral IM increases for a 7-year IRS, MVA increases linearly. KVA under IMM decreases rapidly then levels off. Under IMM there is a net xVA benefit for moderate IM levels — optimal IM is non-zero even before regulatory requirements.

questions.subtopic: Why bilateral IM is not favoured purely by KVA
questions.question: Why would it be considered regulatory arbitrage if banks could justify very high bilateral IM purely based on KVA reduction, without a regulatory mandate?
questions.answer_short: If giving each other capital (IM) were cheaper than holding it themselves, banks would voluntarily over-collateralise to reduce capital requirements — essentially substituting IM for regulatory capital, which was never the regulatory intent.
questions.answer_long: If bilateral IM consistently reduced total xVA (including KVA) enough to justify large voluntary IM postings, banks would have an incentive to post massive IM to each other purely to reduce capital, effectively substituting counterparty-provided collateral for regulatory capital buffers. This would undermine the purpose of capital requirements, which are meant to absorb unexpected losses from equity, not from a counterparty's posted assets. The diminishing returns observed in Figure 16.9 naturally limit this incentive. However, the combination of CVA, FVA, and KVA benefits may collectively make high IM attractive — which is precisely why regulators impose bilateral IM requirements rather than relying purely on incentives.
questions.why_it_matters: This argument is important for understanding regulatory design: IM requirements are mandated rather than purely incentivised because the incentive calculus would not always be strong enough without a mandate.
common_traps: Thinking voluntary IM posting is never optimal — it can be, at moderate levels
Ignoring that regulatory arbitrage concerns are a regulatory design issue, not just a mathematical one
Forgetting that Chapter 19 analyses the combined xVA impact of IM more fully
questions.real_world_example: If banks found that posting $100M IM to each other reduced combined KVA by $200M (net gain $100M), they would voluntarily over-collateralise to arbitrage capital rules — regulators prevent this by mandating IM amounts via SIMM rather than letting banks choose freely.

questions.question: What is the fundamental overlap between CVA and KVA, and how does the max(CVA, EL + KVA) formula attempt to address it?
questions.answer_short: CVA charges for perfect hedging of counterparty risk; KVA charges for holding capital because CVA cannot be perfectly hedged. The max() formula charges the larger of: (a) hedged approach (CVA only, no capital) or (b) warehoused approach (EL + KVA, no hedge).
questions.answer_long: CVA computed with risk-neutral default probabilities is the theoretical cost of perfectly hedging counterparty risk. If perfectly hedged, no capital is required (the hedge eliminates the risk). KVA represents capital required because the hedge is imperfect. These are alternative regimes: if perfectly hedging (CVA approach), capital requirements should be zero (so no KVA); if warehousing risk (no hedge), capital charges apply (KVA) plus an expected loss term (EL, which is CVA under real-world probabilities). The max(CVA, EL + KVA) formula attempts to select the larger of these two extremes. However, this is flawed: an xVA desk operates under limits and cannot fully warehouse risk, and if CVA is charged but not hedged, capital is wasted.
questions.why_it_matters: This overlap is one of the most difficult xVA pricing problems. Double-counting CVA and KVA overstates the cost; ignoring the interaction understates it. A more rigorous approach (Kenyon and Green) charges CVA proportional to hedged fraction and KVA proportional to unhedged fraction.
common_traps: Adding CVA and KVA together without considering the overlap
Assuming the max() formula is theoretically sound — the book explicitly calls it flawed
Ignoring that EL is CVA under real-world (not risk-neutral) parameters
questions.real_world_example: A bank charges max(CVA, EL+KVA) on a corporate swap. CVA (risk-neutral) = 100 bps; EL (real-world) = 40 bps; KVA = 80 bps. EL+KVA = 120 bps > CVA, so the bank charges 120 bps. But then the xVA desk has no cash to hedge the counterparty risk (the 120 bps is earmarked for capital, not hedge premium).

questions.question: How should capital-reducing hedges (e.g., single-name CDS) be incorporated into KVA, and what limits their effectiveness?
questions.answer_short: Hedges that are eligible for capital relief (e.g., single-name CDS) reduce the EC profile in the KVA formula. However, eligibility depends on CDS liquidity, and capital relief is partial — full capital relief requires matching maturity and notional exactly.
questions.answer_long: When a bank hedges CVA with a single-name CDS, this provides capital relief by reducing the CVA capital charge. To correctly capture this in KVA, the reduced EC profile (after hedge) must be used. The challenge is that: (1) not all counterparties have liquid single-name CDS markets — some are illiquid or non-existent; (2) capital relief requires the hedge to be an eligible instrument (correct form and terms); and (3) the extent of relief depends on future CDS market liquidity, which may change. The preferred approach (Kenyon and Green) charges CVA for the proportion of risk hedged and KVA for the unhedged residual, naturally incorporating hedge effectiveness.
questions.why_it_matters: Overestimating capital relief overstates KVA reduction from hedges, while underestimating creates double-counting with CVA. Both lead to mispricing. Understanding what hedges qualify is essential for KVA management.
common_traps: Assuming all CVA hedges qualify for capital relief — only eligible instruments do
Using 100% capital relief for partial hedges
Ignoring that index hedges provide only partial, approximate capital relief
questions.real_world_example: A bank hedges CVA for a single-A corporate client with a single-name CDS. This achieves full capital relief and allows the bank to charge only the CVA component (no KVA). For an illiquid counterparty without a CDS market, no capital relief is possible, so full KVA must be charged alongside CVA.

questions.subtopic: CVA volatility from RWA reduction — unintended consequence
questions.question: What is the unintended accounting consequence of a bank aggressively reducing its counterparty risk capital (RWA reduction programme), as illustrated by a real bank example?
questions.answer_short: Reducing CCR capital through hedges (e.g., CDS) or netting improvements increases CVA hedge effectiveness, which should also reduce CVA hedges. But if done incorrectly, it can increase the volatility of accounting CVA, DVA, and FVA, worsening P&L volatility.
questions.answer_long: A large bank reduced counterparty risk RWA through a deleveraging programme. However, this inadvertently increased the volatility of their accounting CVA (and DVA, FVA) numbers. The reason: counterparty risk hedges that reduced RWA (capital) also changed the composition of the CVA hedge book. When these hedges appeared as naked positions in the market risk capital framework (Section 8.7.5), the bank faced higher market risk capital while having lower CCR capital — the opposite of their intent. This example illustrates the dangerous inconsistency between accounting standards, market risk frameworks, and CVA capital rules that BCBS (2015) proposals aim to address.
questions.why_it_matters: Regulatory capital rules are not always internally consistent with accounting standards or market practices. Banks undertaking capital optimisation programmes must understand these interactions to avoid perverse outcomes.
common_traps: Assuming that reducing CCR capital always reduces total capital — market risk capital may increase
Ignoring accounting CVA volatility implications of capital management actions
Treating capital, accounting, and xVA frameworks as independent when they interact
questions.real_world_example: Carver (2013) documents a major bank's RWA reduction programme that led to increased CVA accounting volatility — a perverse outcome where reducing capital risk metrics worsened P&L risk.

questions.subtopic: KVA as accounting item — arguments for
questions.question: What are three arguments in favour of treating KVA as an accounting adjustment (similar to CVA and FVA), rather than as just a capital hurdle?
questions.answer_short: 1) Returns on capital would be properly amortised over the trade lifetime rather than front-loaded. 2) Front-office incentives would align to long-term profitability. 3) KVA could be transfer-priced to a central xVA desk and managed actively.
questions.answer_long: If KVA were treated as an accounting item: (1) Return on capital: profits could be released over the trade lifetime, generating steady returns rather than a lump at inception followed by zero. Capital hurdles create front-loaded profit recognition that misaligns economic and accounting reality. (2) Incentives: Front-office staff would be incentivised to manage the lifetime costs of trades rather than maximising day-one profits. (3) Management: Like CVA and FVA, KVA could be transfer-priced to a central xVA desk and actively hedged/managed. Without this, volatile regulatory capital (e.g., from large FX moves) hits individual business units unpredictably.
questions.why_it_matters: The debate over KVA accounting treatment mirrors earlier debates about FVA. Resolving it has significant implications for bank earnings reporting, front-office behaviour, and regulatory perception.
common_traps: Assuming KVA accounting treatment is straightforward — the one-off adjustment would be very large for long-dated books
Ignoring that the FVA accounting debate is not yet resolved — KVA treatment depends on it
Thinking competitors would align quickly — the competitive dynamic makes first-mover risk significant
questions.real_world_example: A bank with a large long-dated derivatives book might face a one-time KVA liability several times larger than its reported FVA when transitioning to accounting treatment — a potential shock to reported equity that would require careful communication to shareholders.

questions.question: What are two major obstacles preventing widespread adoption of KVA as a formal accounting adjustment by banks?
questions.answer_short: 1) The one-off accounting adjustment required would be very large (given long-dated books), potentially unacceptable to staff and shareholders. 2) The FVA accounting debate is unresolved — KVA treatment cannot be standardised until FVA accounting issues are settled.
questions.answer_long: First, transitioning to KVA accounting would require an immediate write-down of deferred profits, creating a one-off charge potentially much larger than FVA (which itself was controversial). For banks with large books of long-dated uncollateralised derivatives, this could be very significant. Staff bonuses and capital ratios would be hit immediately. Second, accounting bodies and regulators have not resolved whether FVA should be an accounting adjustment (arguments exist on both sides in Section 15.3.7). Since KVA has similar conceptual challenges to FVA (is it a fair value adjustment or an internal pricing tool?), the FVA debate must be resolved first. Without FVA clarity, KVA accounting treatment remains premature.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding these obstacles explains why KVA remains a pricing tool rather than an accounting item for most banks, and why convergence of market practice will be slow.
common_traps: Assuming KVA accounting treatment is just a technical question — it is also a business and regulatory one
Ignoring competitive dynamics — if only some banks adopt accounting KVA, they are disadvantaged
Treating FVA and KVA accounting debates as independent
questions.real_world_example: JPMorgan's recognition of FVA in 2014 ($1.5B charge) was controversial and created competitive concerns. A similar or larger KVA recognition would face even greater scrutiny from shareholders, auditors, and regulators.

questions.subtopic: IM profile changes and portfolio composition
questions.question: How can the projected IM profile for a portfolio actually increase over time, contrary to the simple decay expected for a single transaction?
questions.answer_short: When trades that are currently offsetting (hedging) longer-dated trades mature and drop out of the portfolio, the remaining portfolio loses diversification and IM can increase. Portfolio IM is non-monotonic unlike single-trade IM.
questions.answer_long: For a single transaction with periodic cashflows, the IM profile decays monotonically to zero as maturity approaches. For a portfolio, however, transactions mature at different times. If a short-dated transaction is currently offsetting (reducing portfolio VAR relative to) a longer-dated transaction, when the short-dated trade matures and exits the portfolio, the portfolio IM can jump upward since the offsetting effect is lost. This non-monotonic behaviour makes portfolio IM projection complex and cannot be captured by single-trade approximations.
questions.why_it_matters: Pricing MVA using single-trade IM profiles rather than portfolio IM profiles can significantly underestimate future IM requirements, particularly when hedging transactions are included in the portfolio.
common_traps: Assuming portfolio IM decays like single-trade IM
Ignoring the impact of hedging transactions that expire before the main portfolio
Treating portfolio IM as the sum of individual trade IMs
questions.real_world_example: A bank has a 10-year receiver swap (creates positive MTM in rising rates) and a 5-year payer swap (creates positive MTM in falling rates). When the 5-year payer expires, the 10-year receiver's IM requirement jumps upward because the offsetting payer is gone.

questions.question: How does received IM contribute to MVA, and why is this sometimes overlooked?
questions.answer_short: Received IM must typically be segregated, creating a segregation cost (the cost of holding it in a segregated account at low yield rather than deploying it). This cost appears as an MVA adjustment on the reverse portfolio.
questions.answer_long: When a bank receives IM, it cannot freely use those assets (they must be held in a segregated account for the benefit of the poster). The bank must therefore hold assets that earn a low segregated return rather than the bank's usual funding rate. This segregation cost is a form of MVA on the received side, computed on the reverse portfolio (the notional IM expected to be received). The total MVA should therefore include both posted IM cost and received IM segregation cost. This bidirectional nature of MVA is often overlooked by practitioners who focus only on posting costs.
questions.why_it_matters: Ignoring received IM costs understates total MVA. For dealers who are net receivers of IM (from client portfolios), this can be a material omission.
common_traps: Treating received IM as zero cost because the bank 'holds' it
Forgetting that segregation prevents deployment of received IM at market rates
Ignoring received IM MVA in the total xVA calculation
questions.real_world_example: A prime broker receiving $500M IM from a hedge fund client must hold it segregated. At 1.5% opportunity cost (funding rate minus segregated return), the annual segregation cost is $7.5M — an MVA charge that should reduce the prime brokerage spread charged to the client.

questions.question: Why is computing the expected capital profile for the IMM approach significantly more computationally challenging than for CEM or SA-CCR?
questions.answer_short: IMM itself is a Monte Carlo-based method. Simulating future IMM capital requires running a Monte Carlo at each node of an outer Monte Carlo — a nested simulation problem orders of magnitude more expensive than analytical CEM or SA-CCR formulas.
questions.answer_long: CEM and SA-CCR capital charges are computed using closed-form formulas (simple add-ons and sensitivity-based multipliers). Running these formulas along exposure simulation paths is straightforward. IMM capital, however, requires its own Monte Carlo simulation to determine the EE, EPE, and capital charge at each future time point. To compute the expected IMM capital across all future scenarios requires running an inner Monte Carlo at each node of an outer Monte Carlo — the nested simulation problem. As a result, exact expected IMM capital is computationally intractable for large portfolios, and banks typically use the projected (deterministic) capital as a proxy, which — as Figure 16.7 shows — is a reasonable approximation since CEM introduces most of the asymmetry.
questions.why_it_matters: This explains why banks with IMM approval often use simpler KVA approximations despite having sophisticated exposure models. The computational limit of nested Monte Carlo is a fundamental constraint in xVA management.
common_traps: Assuming IMM always gives the most accurate KVA — it may only be approximated
Thinking the projected IMM capital is always close to expected — it is for symmetric exposures
Ignoring that approximation quality degrades for portfolios with significant optionality
questions.real_world_example: A bank with IMM approval attempts to compute KVA by running the IMM model at 1,000 future scenario nodes monthly for 10 years. With 100,000 inner scenarios per node, the total simulation count is 120 × 100,000 × 1,000 = 12 billion — infeasible in production timescales.

questions.question: Why does the increasing use of risk-sensitive IM methodologies like SIMM make MVA computationally more challenging than when IM was based on simple notional percentages?
questions.answer_short: SIMM computes IM based on option sensitivities (Greeks) across multiple risk factors, making IM path-dependent and requiring the full sensitivity calculation at each future scenario node — far more expensive than a simple notional multiplier.
questions.answer_long: Historically, IM was a simple percentage of notional (e.g., 2% of notional for a 5-year IRS). Computing projected IM was trivial: just multiply the notional by the percentage. SIMM (Section 6.7.7), however, computes IM based on risk factor sensitivities (delta, vega, curvature) aggregated across multiple asset classes and cross-bucket correlations. At each future scenario node in the exposure simulation, SIMM requires computing all relevant Greeks for the entire portfolio — a computationally intensive operation. When combined with the outer Monte Carlo for exposure, this creates a significant nested computation challenge, which is the main practical barrier to accurate SIMM-based MVA.
questions.why_it_matters: The industry shift toward risk-sensitive IM (SIMM, CCP models) directly drives MVA computation complexity. Banks that cannot compute SIMM-based MVA accurately will systematically misprize new trades.
common_traps: Thinking SIMM-based MVA can use simple notional-based proxy calculations
Ignoring the cross-bucket correlation effects in SIMM that make portfolio IM non-linear
Assuming that delta approximations are sufficient for SIMM-based MVA at 99% confidence levels
questions.real_world_example: A bank pricing MVA on an exotic rate option portfolio under SIMM must compute vega sensitivities to 30+ volatility surface points at each of 10,000 scenario nodes across 120 monthly time steps — a massive computation requiring specialised numerical methods or AMC.

questions.question: Why does CEM not benefit from received IM in the KVA calculation, and how does this compare to SA-CCR and IMM?
questions.answer_short: CEM does not formally recognise received IM as reducing exposure — it uses a simple add-on that doesn't reflect actual collateral. SA-CCR and IMM properly recognise received IM, reducing the capital charge and thus KVA.
questions.answer_long: CEM calculates capital using replacement cost (max(MTM,0)) plus a simple notional-based add-on. It does not incorporate received IM as an offset to exposure in its formula (apart from reducing replacement cost to near zero if the IM covers the current MTM). SA-CCR explicitly includes IM in the net replacement cost calculation, so received IM directly reduces the exposure and capital charge. IMM also recognises received IM through reduced EE in the exposure simulation. This is why Figure 16.9 shows that KVA (CEM) is flat as bilateral IM increases — the capital does not decrease because CEM cannot capture the IM benefit — while KVA (IMM) and KVA (SA-CCR) decline as IM increases.
questions.why_it_matters: Banks using CEM receive no KVA benefit from accepting IM, which distorts the cost-benefit analysis of bilateral IM. This is one of the well-documented flaws of CEM and a reason regulators are phasing it out in favour of SA-CCR.
common_traps: Assuming all capital methodologies equally recognise received IM
Using CEM for IM-sensitive portfolios and expecting capital reduction
Ignoring that CEM's inability to recognise IM means KVA is overestimated for IM-receiving banks using CEM
questions.real_world_example: A bank using CEM receives $50M IM from a counterparty on a $200M notional swap. The CEM capital charge barely changes (only replacement cost drops), while under SA-CCR the full IM is recognised in the net replacement cost, materially reducing the capital charge and KVA.

questions.subtopic: Increased complexity of IM and capital methodologies
questions.question: Why does the shift towards risk-sensitive IM and capital methodologies (SIMM, IMM) make MVA and KVA significantly harder to compute?
questions.answer_short: Risk-sensitive methods require projecting the output of complex models at every future date, creating a 'simulation of simulations' problem. Simple notional-based methods could be projected analytically, but SIMM and IMM require numerical evaluation at each future node.
questions.answer_long: When IM is a fixed percentage of notional, projecting IM through time is trivial — just scale the known notional schedule. Similarly, when capital uses a simple formula (CEM add-ons), projecting capital is straightforward. However, SIMM calculates IM from risk sensitivities that vary with market moves, and IMM calculates capital from a full exposure simulation. At each future time point, to compute EIM or EC, the model must evaluate the complex methodology — SIMM or IMM — in each scenario. This requires running the exact or approximate version of the methodology at thousands of future scenario points, creating the nested computation challenges that are central to modern MVA and KVA implementation.
questions.why_it_matters: This is the core challenge of modern xVA management: as regulatory methods become more risk-sensitive, they also become more expensive to project, driving the need for numerical methods like American Monte Carlo.
common_traps: Assuming that using simple approximations (delta-gamma for SIMM) is always accurate enough
Treating IM projection as a simple scaling problem when SIMM is used
Ignoring that methodology changes (e.g., CEM to SA-CCR) also require updating KVA calculations
questions.real_world_example: The shift from CEM to SA-CCR at a bank requires recalculating the entire KVA portfolio using SA-CCR formulas at each future scenario node — a significant one-time computational project that must be operationally completed before the regulatory transition date.

questions.question: Why do cross-currency swaps have approximately flat capital profiles similar to FX forwards, and how does this affect KVA?
questions.answer_short: Cross-currency swaps involve exchange of principals in different currencies at maturity, creating large terminal cash flows. Like FX forwards, this keeps the exposure and capital approximately flat. Periodic interest cashflows cause slight amortisation but the FX principal dominates.
questions.answer_long: A cross-currency swap involves notional exchanges at inception and maturity in two currencies, plus periodic interest payments. The large FX-driven principal repayment at maturity dominates the exposure profile, keeping it approximately flat through the transaction lifetime (similar to an FX forward). The periodic interest cashflows cause some modest amortisation (unlike a pure FX forward). This flat profile means capital under any methodology remains elevated through the trade's life, producing a relatively high KVA compared to a same-maturity IRS. This is a key pricing consideration for cross-currency products.
questions.why_it_matters: Mispricing cross-currency swap KVA by using an IRS-like amortising profile significantly underestimates the capital cost. Given the large notional principals involved, the error can be material.
common_traps: Applying an IRS-like decaying capital profile to cross-currency swaps
Ignoring the terminal principal exchange as the dominant exposure driver
Assuming cross-currency IRS and plain IRS have similar KVA
questions.real_world_example: A 10-year USD/JPY cross-currency swap has approximately flat capital through its life due to the USD notional repayment at maturity. A 10-year USD IRS has decaying capital. The cross-currency swap KVA may be 50-70% larger despite similar notional amounts.

questions.question: How can the leverage ratio constrain bank balance sheets in a way that affects KVA, and why was this particularly uncertain at the time of writing?
questions.answer_short: The leverage ratio limits total assets relative to equity, constraining the ability to take on new exposures regardless of risk sensitivity. It can become the binding capital constraint for derivatives-heavy banks, making it a significant KVA driver — but its final calibration (3% in Europe, 4-6% in US) was not yet set in 2015.
questions.answer_long: The leverage ratio is a blunt capital tool that does not differentiate between high-risk and low-risk exposures — it limits total (gross or semi-gross) exposures relative to equity. For a derivatives-heavy bank, this can be more constraining than risk-based capital (CCR charge). When the leverage ratio is binding, adding any new transaction — even low-risk ones — requires more equity. KVA must capture this leverage ratio cost, which depends on the balance sheet exposure contribution of the trade (SA-CCR or simpler measures). At the time of writing, the leverage ratio was 3% in Europe but not yet finalised, with the US considering 4-6%, creating substantial KVA uncertainty for banks estimating long-dated costs.
questions.why_it_matters: The leverage ratio can dominate KVA for low-margin, large-notional trades (like IRS) where risk-based capital is low but notional-based leverage ratio capital is high. Ignoring it understates KVA for these trades.
common_traps: Treating leverage ratio as a minor add-on to risk-based capital
Using the European 3% figure for US clients when the US rate is higher
Forgetting that leverage ratio uncertainty makes long-dated KVA projections very imprecise
questions.real_world_example: A dealer bank finds that for large vanilla IRS trades, the leverage ratio (requiring more equity per $ of notional) is more constraining than the CCR capital charge. The KVA from the leverage ratio alone can exceed the risk-based capital KVA for some trade types.

questions.subtopic: Market practice on contingent IM pricing
questions.question: According to the Solum CVA survey 2015, what does market practice show about how banks treat contingent IM requirements in pricing?
questions.answer_short: Market practice is divided: some banks ignore contingent IM entirely, others price based on current ratings only (no contingent component), and many price using credit rating migration probabilities or assume the downgrade trigger is always breached (per LCR requirements).
questions.answer_long: Figure 16.1 shows that market practice on contingent IM pricing is split across multiple approaches: (1) No pricing of contingent requirements at all; (2) Pricing based on current rating only, ignoring the contingent scenario; (3) Pricing based on credit rating migration probabilities to estimate the expected contingent cost; (4) Assuming the trigger is always breached (fully pricing the contingent IM, consistent with LCR requirements). Many banks, especially regarding their own potential downgrade, do price in these costs. The split in practice creates price divergence, similar to the divergence seen in KVA treatment.
questions.why_it_matters: Banks that ignore contingent IM costs may appear more competitive in pricing but are systematically under-reserved for liquidity events. Understanding market practice helps assess where a bank's pricing stands relative to peers.
common_traps: Assuming all banks price contingent IM consistently
Thinking LCR requires banks to price based on current ratings only
Ignoring that counterparty downgrade triggers (counterparty rating) are treated differently from own-rating downgrade triggers
questions.real_world_example: Bank A assumes downgrade triggers are never breached and prices MVA without contingent component. Bank B assumes full LCR compliance and prices the full contingent cost. For the same trade, Bank A's price is 5 bps lower — but Bank A is underprepared for a downgrade liquidity event.

questions.question: How do CVA capital exemptions in Europe affect KVA, and why does the potential reversal of these exemptions create significant pricing uncertainty?
questions.answer_short: European banks with CVA exemptions (for sovereigns, pensions, NFCs) face much lower CVA capital charges, substantially reducing their KVA relative to non-exempt banks. A reversal of exemptions could multiply KVA for these counterparty types by 5-10x.
questions.answer_long: As discussed in Section 8.7.7, European banks currently enjoy exemptions from the CVA capital charge for many counterparty types including sovereigns, pension funds, and non-financial counterparties (NFCs). This dramatically reduces CVA capital and hence KVA for trades with these counterparties. If these exemptions are reversed (either locally by regulators or via EU-wide rule changes), the CVA capital charge would apply to all such trades, potentially increasing KVA by an order of magnitude for sovereign and NFC counterparties. This uncertainty makes pricing long-dated trades with these counterparty types extremely sensitive to regulatory assumptions, and explains why some banks price conservatively (assuming eventual reversal) while others price optimistically (assuming exemptions persist).
questions.why_it_matters: A reversal of CVA exemptions could make European dealer banks significantly less competitive for trades with sovereign and pension fund counterparties compared to US banks (which have no such exemptions to lose). Pricing incorrectly can lead to material losses when the regulatory change occurs.
common_traps: Assuming CVA exemptions are permanent in Europe
Treating exempt and non-exempt counterparties with the same KVA model
Underestimating the KVA impact of exemption reversal for long-dated sovereign trades
questions.real_world_example: A European bank pricing a 20-year IRS with a sovereign counterparty under current exemptions charges minimal CVA capital KVA. If exemptions are reversed, the CVA capital charge could require 10x more capital, making the historic KVA charge drastically insufficient.

questions.question: Under what maturity conditions is posting initial margin more beneficial than operating under an FCA-only (uncollateralised) framework, and what drives this relationship?
questions.answer_short: IM posting becomes more favourable for longer-dated transactions. This is because IM shortens the effective funding time horizon from the trade's full maturity to just the IM time horizon (10 days), and this shortening is more valuable for longer maturities.
questions.answer_long: The approximate relationship between MVA and FCA (Equation 16.2) shows that MVA is approximately proportional to √(τIM/T), where τIM is the IM time horizon (10 days) and T is the trade maturity. For long-dated trades (large T), the square root term is small, making MVA much lower than FCA. For short-dated trades (small T), the two become comparable. Additionally, longer-dated trades also benefit more from the CVA reduction that comes with IM posting (because the credit risk is larger for longer maturities). Therefore, IM is more attractive (vs FCA) for longer-dated transactions and vice versa for shorter ones.
