Therefore, the day-1 capital charge is the same for collateralised and uncollateralised trades. The difference emerges as the trade ages: in the collateralised case, variation margin continuously reduces the exposure to within the MPR horizon, keeping capital low. In the uncollateralised case, the exposure grows with market moves over the full remaining maturity. For the spot capital in Table 16.2, the collateralised projected KVA is -0.457 for all three methodologies — equal to the uncollateralised CEM projected, but different from SA-CCR and IMM projected, reflecting the different starting capital assumptions.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding that capital benefits of collateral emerge over time (not immediately) is important for intra-day risk management and for understanding why new trades may have high capital on day one before collateral is established.
common_traps: Assuming collateralised trades have zero capital — they have MPR-based capital
Forgetting that the spot capital is the same for both at inception
Confusing projected capital (deterministic) with actual capital (path-dependent)
questions.real_world_example: A bank prices an uncollateralised swap at inception with the same spot capital as a collateralised one. Over time, the uncollateralised capital grows while the collateralised stays low (at 10-day MPR capital). The KVA differential builds gradually, not on day one.

questions.question: Why will MVA become increasingly important in the future according to the chapter summary, and what are the two main regulatory drivers?
questions.answer_short: MVA will grow in importance as (1) clearing mandates expand, requiring more CCP IM, and (2) bilateral BCBS-IOSCO IM rules phase in, requiring IM posting on all non-cleared trades. Both increase the total IM in the system substantially.
questions.answer_long: The chapter summary notes that MVA 'will become increasingly important in the future in determining the cost of posting' IM. The two drivers are: (1) Central clearing mandates: as more products are mandated to clear, more IM must be posted to CCPs. The clearing mandate has been expanding to cover interest rate swaps, credit default swaps, and potentially other asset classes. (2) Bilateral BCBS-IOSCO IM rules: effective from September 2016, requiring IM posting on all non-cleared OTC derivatives above a threshold. As more counterparties fall within scope (due to phase-in thresholds decreasing over time), bilateral IM requirements grow. Together, these increase total system-wide IM substantially, making MVA a material pricing consideration for almost all OTC derivatives.
questions.why_it_matters: The forward-looking nature of MVA's importance means that banks must build MVA infrastructure now, even if current trades have limited IM. As the regulatory landscape matures, MVA will be as standard as CVA in derivative pricing.
common_traps: Assuming MVA only matters for cleared trades — bilateral IM rules make it universal
Thinking MVA is a one-time issue once trades are priced at inception — it requires ongoing management as IM changes
Ignoring the phase-in schedule for bilateral IM (different threshold amounts per year)
questions.real_world_example: In 2015, only a small fraction of bilateral trades were subject to mandatory IM. By 2022, with phase 6 of BCBS-IOSCO IM rules covering almost all counterparties above a minimal threshold, MVA became relevant for the vast majority of OTC derivative trades globally.

questions.subtopic: Survival probability in KVA vs MVA
questions.question: How does the survival probability function serve the same role in both the MVA and KVA formulas, and what is the key difference in its interpretation?
questions.answer_short: Both formulas use S(t) to discount future costs by the probability that the transaction is still active (both parties alive). In MVA, default ends IM posting (IM returned). In KVA, default ends the capital requirement (transaction terminated). The S(t) function reflects joint survival in both cases.
questions.answer_long: In both formulas — MVA = −∑ EIM(t) × FC_net × Δt × S(t) and KVA = −∑ EC(t) × CC × Δt × S(t) — the survival probability S(t) reflects the probability that both parties have survived to time t. For MVA, this is appropriate because IM is returned upon default — if either party defaults early, the IM posting costs stop. For KVA, capital requirements cease upon default — if the bank defaults, it no longer needs to hold regulatory capital. In both cases, S(t) should represent the joint survival of both parties (bank and counterparty), though in practice the bank's own default may be treated differently under DVA considerations.
questions.why_it_matters: The shared survival probability structure across xVA components (CVA, MVA, KVA) provides a unified mathematical framework. Understanding this allows practitioners to use the same survival probability term consistently across all adjustments.
common_traps: Using only the counterparty's survival probability when the joint survival is appropriate
Treating S(t) differently in MVA vs KVA when the same function applies
Forgetting that the bank's own default probability enters through S(t) and may need DVA-consistent treatment
questions.real_world_example: For a 10-year IRS with a single-A counterparty, S(t) decays from 1.0 at t=0 to approximately 0.85 at t=10 (15% probability of default). This reduces both MVA and KVA by about 7-8% relative to a calculation ignoring survival, since future costs are probability-weighted by S(t).

questions.subtopic: RWA reduction and CVA volatility paradox
questions.question: Explain the paradox: how can reducing counterparty risk capital (CCR RWA) actually increase accounting CVA volatility, as experienced by a major bank (Carver 2013)?
questions.answer_short: When a bank reduces CCR RWA by unwinding or hedging derivatives, it may reduce its CVA hedge book (CDS protection) simultaneously. With fewer CDS hedges, the CVA becomes less hedged, meaning credit spread movements create larger P&L swings in the accounting CVA.
questions.answer_long: A bank's CCR RWA is reduced by: (1) reducing gross exposures (unwinding trades); (2) improving netting; (3) buying CDS protection on counterparties. When option (3) is used heavily, the bank has large CDS positions that offset counterparty risk capital. However, if the CDS are treating as capital hedges (reducing CCR RWA) rather than accounting CVA hedges, the accounting CVA may not be fully delta-hedged by the same CDS. When the bank then sells some CDS (as part of the RWA reduction programme), the accounting CVA hedge ratio falls, increasing sensitivity to credit spread moves. The result: lower CCR capital but higher accounting CVA volatility — an unintended trade-off between regulatory capital and accounting P&L.
questions.why_it_matters: This real-world case illustrates that regulatory capital management and accounting CVA management are not automatically aligned. Banks must carefully coordinate CCR capital hedges with accounting CVA hedges to avoid this paradox.
common_traps: Assuming regulatory capital hedges and accounting CVA hedges are equivalent
Thinking reducing CCR RWA always improves all risk metrics
Ignoring that accounting CVA volatility can increase even when regulatory capital decreases
questions.real_world_example: The Carver (2013) article documented a major bank that reported significant CVA accounting losses during its RWA reduction programme — directly contradicting the narrative that capital reduction improves the institution's risk profile.

questions.subtopic: MVA benefits of IM for longer maturities
questions.question: A corporate client asks why the bank is recommending clearing for a 10-year swap but not for a 1-year swap. What xVA-based argument supports this recommendation?
questions.answer_short: For the 10-year swap, clearing's IM replaces multi-year unsecured FCA with a 10-day IM cost — a large saving (FCA >> MVA for long maturities). For the 1-year swap, the time horizons are comparable and FCA is small, so the clearing infrastructure cost outweighs the MVA saving.
questions.answer_long: From the MVA/FCA approximation, MVA ≈ FCA × √(τIM/T) × Φ⁻¹(α)/φ(0). For a 10-year swap (T=2500 days, τIM=10 days), the factor is √(10/2500) × 5.8 ≈ 0.46 — meaning MVA is less than half of FCA. The saving from replacing FCA with MVA is substantial. For a 1-year swap (T=250 days, τIM=10 days), the factor is √(10/250) × 5.8 ≈ 1.46 — meaning MVA exceeds FCA by ~46%. Clearing actually costs more than going uncollateralised for short-dated trades. Additionally, clearing involves membership costs and operational overhead that are relatively larger for small short-dated trades.
questions.why_it_matters: This analysis directly informs execution decisions: clearing is most beneficial for long-dated transactions and potentially counterproductive for short-dated ones. Banks and clients should use this framework to optimise clearing decisions.
common_traps: Recommending clearing for all maturities uniformly
Ignoring CCP membership and operational costs in the clearing vs bilateral comparison
Applying the approximation to products with very different risk profiles without adjustment
questions.real_world_example: A corporate treasury executing both a 10-year and a 1-year IRS benefits from clearing the 10-year (large FCA saving) but should evaluate carefully whether to clear the 1-year given the higher relative MVA and overhead costs.

questions.question: What are 'output floors' for IMM banks, why were they proposed, and how do they affect KVA calculations?
questions.answer_short: Output floors set a minimum regulatory capital level as a percentage of the standardised approach (SA-CCR) capital for IMM banks. They prevent IMM models from producing unrealistically low capital. They increase EC for IMM banks where the floor is binding, raising KVA.
questions.answer_long: Output floors (proposed in BCBS documents) require that the capital calculated using internal models (IMM) must not fall below a specified percentage (e.g., 72.5% under Basel IV) of the capital calculated using standardised approaches (SA-CCR). This prevents banks from using sophisticated internal models to dramatically reduce capital relative to simple standardised calculations — a concern that IMM models might be optimised to minimise regulatory capital rather than to accurately measure risk. For KVA purposes, if the IMM-based capital falls below the floor, the effective EC is the floor (based on SA-CCR), raising KVA above the pure IMM level. Banks with IMM must model whether the floor is binding throughout the trade's life.
questions.why_it_matters: Output floors were among the most debated elements of Basel IV. Their implementation changes the relative attractiveness of IMM approval and increases KVA for banks where the floor is binding — representing a convergence of IMM and standardised KVA.
common_traps: Assuming IMM always gives the lowest capital after output floors — the floor may make SA-CCR binding
Ignoring that floors are phased in (not immediately binding at full level)
Treating output floor implementation as certain — at the time of writing, exact parameters were not finalised
questions.real_world_example: A bank with IMM approval computes KVA using IMM capital = 60 (units). SA-CCR capital = 100. With a 72.5% floor, the effective capital = max(60, 72.5) = 72.5. KVA must be computed using 72.5, not 60 — the floor raises the KVA charge by approximately 20% for this trade.

questions.question: What are the alternatives to posting contingent IM under a ratings downgrade trigger, and why is each alternative potentially more expensive or difficult to quantify?
questions.answer_short: Alternatives include: (1) Transaction termination (costly if replacement pricing is adverse); (2) Substitution with a higher-rated entity (guarantee or novation); (3) Voluntary pre-posting of IM to remove the trigger. Each has costs that are difficult to quantify ex-ante.
questions.answer_long: When a ratings downgrade triggers IM posting, a firm may have several alternatives: (1) Transaction termination: the triggered party may exercise a right to terminate, but the replacement cost (price from a new counterparty) may be higher than the contingent IM cost — particularly difficult to estimate in advance. (2) Novation to a higher-rated entity: substituting a higher-rated subsidiary or guarantor to avoid triggering the provision — requires legal restructuring with associated costs. (3) Voluntary pre-posting of IM: proactively posting IM to have the downgrade trigger removed from the CSA, making the IM non-contingent. The book notes that voluntary pre-posting may actually be cheaper if the posted IM must already be held as HQLA under LCR anyway. The difficulty is that these alternatives are path-dependent and hard to price at inception.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding alternatives to contingent IM helps desks structure trades that minimise total MVA cost. The voluntary pre-posting option is particularly interesting because it converts an uncertain contingent cost into a known certain cost.
common_traps: Assuming contingent IM must always be posted at trigger — alternatives exist
Ignoring the replacement pricing risk when termination is the alternative
Not considering that voluntary pre-posting may be cheaper than maintaining a liquidity buffer
questions.real_world_example: A bank with a 2-notch downgrade trigger on a large bilateral netting set evaluates whether to proactively post $100M IM to remove the trigger. If the HQLA needed for LCR would cost $1M/year, and the voluntary IM would only cost $0.8M/year (lower spread since it's now non-contingent), pre-posting is preferable.

questions.question: How would KVA accounting treatment change the timing of profit recognition for a derivatives desk, and why is this more economically correct?
questions.answer_short: Currently, all derivative profit is recognised at inception (day-one P&L). With KVA accounting, profit would be released gradually over the trade lifetime as capital costs are earned back. This matches economic reality: the bank earns returns by providing services over the trade's life.
questions.answer_long: Under current hurdle rate treatment, a derivative with a high enough return on capital is accepted, and all profit is immediately recognised in the trading desk's P&L. The capital is held throughout the life but the profit is front-loaded. With KVA accounting treatment: (1) A KVA liability is recognised at inception (reducing day-one profit); (2) The KVA liability is unwound as capital is released over time, generating steady P&L; (3) The annual KVA release equals approximately CC × EC(t), providing a return on the capital committed in each year. This mirrors how insurance companies amortise premiums, or how banks amortise loan origination fees — matching revenue to the period of service provision.
questions.why_it_matters: The profit release mechanism is the key economic argument for KVA accounting treatment. Without it, trading desks are incentivised to do high-upfront-profit, capital-intensive trades that generate nothing over their life — a classic 'write now, worry later' incentive problem.
common_traps: Assuming KVA accounting creates more total profit — it doesn't, it just redistributes it through time
Thinking KVA accounting is purely an accounting change — it fundamentally changes incentive structures
Ignoring that KVA accounting requires daily marking of the KVA liability, adding operational overhead
questions.real_world_example: Under current practice: a dealer books a 10-year swap on day 1 with $5M profit and $1M KVA charge (hurdle). Day-1 P&L = $4M. With KVA accounting: day-1 P&L = $4M - $5M KVA liability = -$1M, but over 10 years, $500K/year is released from KVA provision, giving steady annual income.

questions.question: In Table 16.2, the CEM collateralised projected KVA equals the CEM uncollateralised projected KVA (-0.457). Why, and what does this reveal about CEM's limitations?
questions.answer_short: CEM's replacement cost is max(MTM,0) — which for an at-market trade is zero, so capital is driven purely by the notional-based add-on regardless of collateral. Collateral doesn't reduce the CEM add-on, so capital and KVA are the same whether or not the trade is collateralised (in the projected case).
questions.answer_long: Under CEM, capital = max(MTM, 0) + Add-On, where Add-On is a fixed percentage of notional. For an at-market swap, MTM = 0, so capital = Add-On, which is the same whether or not collateral is held. Holding collateral would reduce max(MTM,0) for off-market swaps (where MTM > 0), but not for the Add-On component. Since the Add-On is purely notional-based, it is unchanged by collateral. Therefore, CEM gives the same projected capital for collateralised and uncollateralised trades at inception — an obvious flaw. This is why CEM is being replaced by SA-CCR and IMM, which properly recognise collateral in the capital calculation (as seen in Table 16.2 where SA-CCR and IMM give significantly lower collateralised KVA).
questions.why_it_matters: This CEM anomaly directly demonstrates why CEM is an inadequate capital methodology for collateralised portfolios. It creates a disincentive to collateralise (no capital benefit) that is economically perverse and contrary to the regulatory goal of reducing systemic risk.
common_traps: Expecting CEM to give lower KVA for collateralised trades — it doesn't in the projected case
Assuming the add-on in CEM is sensitive to collateral posted
Ignoring that CEM's inability to recognise collateral was a key driver of SA-CCR development
questions.real_world_example: Table 16.2: CEM uncollateralised projected = -0.457; CEM collateralised projected = -0.457. The identical values confirm that CEM provides zero KVA benefit for collateralisation — a fundamental flaw that makes CEM unreliable for pricing decisions involving collateral strategies.

questions.question: Why is MVA always negative (a cost to the bank), and under what circumstances could a bank have a net MVA benefit?
questions.answer_short: MVA is negative because IM posting is always a net cost — the bank funds at above-risk-free rates but earns only at or below risk-free on posted IM. A net MVA benefit would require earning above funding cost on IM, which is generally prohibited by segregation rules.
questions.answer_long: MVA = −∑ EIM × (FC − sIM) × Δt × S(t). FC (funding cost) > sIM (IM remuneration) always, since IM earns risk-free or below while the bank funds at credit-spread above risk-free. Therefore (FC − sIM) > 0 and the negative sign makes MVA negative. A net MVA 'benefit' would require FC < sIM, which would mean the IM earns more than the bank's funding cost. This could theoretically occur if the bank's funding cost is extremely low (e.g., central bank funding at zero) while IM earns above market, but this is not realistic under normal circumstances. Note that received IM also creates a cost (segregation), so there is no obvious path to a net MVA benefit.
questions.why_it_matters: Recognising that MVA is always a cost (never a benefit) is important for the sign convention in pricing. It also reinforces that IM requirements are pure costs from a funding perspective, with any offsetting benefits (reduced CVA, reduced KVA) captured elsewhere in the xVA framework.
common_traps: Confusing the sign convention and treating MVA as a positive (benefit)
Thinking received IM creates a negative MVA (benefit) — it creates an additional cost from segregation
Forgetting that the funding benefit of received IM exists only if the IM can be rehypothecated
questions.real_world_example: A bank posts IM at 1.5% cost and earns 0.5% on the segregated assets — net cost 1.0%. MVA is negative. If a special government facility allowed IM remuneration at 2% (above funding), MVA could theoretically become positive — but this is not a real-world scenario under standard CCP and bilateral rules.

questions.question: Describe the three main positions on how to discount the expected capital profile EC(t) in the KVA formula, and the argument for each.
questions.answer_short: 1) Discount at cost of capital (CC): EC represents foregone equity investments earning CC. 2) Discount at risk-free rate: EC is a regulatory liability, discounted like other regulatory obligations. 3) No discounting: capital requirements are reported at face value, not present value.
questions.answer_long: The KVA formula requires discounting EC(t) to a present value. Three schools exist: (1) Discount at CC (cost of capital): since capital earns CC for shareholders, future capital requirements should be valued at CC — this is the most common traditional approach. (2) Discount at risk-free rate: capital is a regulatory requirement analogous to a liability discounted at the risk-free rate, consistent with how regulatory requirements are generally measured. (3) No discounting: capital ratios are reported at face value without discounting; to be consistent, KVA should use undiscounted EC. The choice can change KVA magnitude by 20-40% for long-dated trades, representing a significant source of pricing subjectivity.
questions.why_it_matters: The discounting debate has no industry consensus and is a source of significant KVA divergence. Banks must make an explicit choice and document the rationale, as it directly affects pricing competitiveness.
common_traps: Assuming there is one correct discount rate for EC
Conflating the EC discount rate with the CC multiplier (they are separate choices)
Using the OIS discount rate for EC without considering whether this is consistent with the KVA purpose
questions.real_world_example: Two dealers price the same 20-year KVA: Dealer A uses CC=10% to discount EC (lower PV of distant capital), Dealer B uses risk-free rate of 2% (higher PV of distant capital). For a steeply amortising EC profile, Dealer A's KVA may be 30% lower than Dealer B's — a major competitive difference for long-dated trades.

questions.question: Why is the EIM for a new trade in a portfolio context potentially very different from the standalone EIM of that trade, and what are the implications for incremental MVA pricing?
questions.answer_short: Portfolio IM benefits from diversification between trades. Adding a trade that is negatively correlated with existing portfolio risk can reduce or even eliminate marginal IM. Conversely, a correlated trade increases portfolio IM. Incremental MVA = portfolio EIM change, not standalone EIM.
questions.answer_long: Within an asset class (e.g., rates), SIMM and CCP IM models allow netting of opposite risk positions. A new receiver swap in a portfolio of existing payer swaps reduces portfolio DV01, reducing portfolio VAR and IM. In this case, the incremental EIM (and hence MVA) for the new trade is much less than its standalone IM — potentially zero or even negative (the new trade actually reduces IM). Conversely, a new payer added to a portfolio of payers adds DV01, increasing portfolio IM by more than the standalone IM due to the loss of diversification. This non-linearity makes incremental MVA highly portfolio-dependent and requires full portfolio recomputation.
questions.why_it_matters: Pricing incremental MVA based on standalone IM can be drastically wrong — either overpricing (for diversifying trades) or underpricing (for concentrating trades). Accurate incremental MVA requires portfolio-level computation, which is computationally intensive.
common_traps: Computing standalone MVA for new trades without portfolio context
Assuming incremental EIM is always between 0 and standalone EIM — it can exceed standalone EIM for concentrating trades
Forgetting that netting only applies within an asset class for bilateral IM
questions.real_world_example: A dealer has a large portfolio of receiver swaps. A client wants to add a large payer swap. The standalone IM for the payer is $5M. But because it offsets $50M of existing receiver DV01, the incremental portfolio IM is actually -$3M (the portfolio IM decreases). The incremental MVA is negative — the client should receive an MVA benefit, not pay one.

questions.question: From a total xVA perspective (CVA + FVA + MVA + KVA), what factors determine the optimal level of bilateral IM for an OTC derivative transaction?
questions.answer_short: Optimal IM minimises total xVA = CVA + FVA + MVA + KVA. Each unit of IM reduces CVA (less credit exposure) and KVA (less capital), while increasing MVA (more IM funding cost) and reducing FBA (less funding benefit). The optimum depends on the trade's maturity, credit quality, and cost of capital.
questions.answer_long: Total xVA = CVA + DVA + FVA(FCA-FBA) + MVA + KVA. Adding IM: reduces CVA (IM protects against credit loss), reduces FCA (less unsecured exposure), eliminates FBA (no funding benefit from negative MTM), increases MVA (IM posting cost), reduces KVA (less capital required), and creates received-IM segregation cost. The optimal IM equates marginal (CVA+FCA+KVA) reduction to marginal (MVA+lost FBA) increase. This optimum depends on: trade maturity (longer → more benefit from IM), counterparty credit quality (riskier → higher CVA, more benefit from IM), cost of capital (higher CC → more KVA, more benefit from IM), and funding cost (higher FC → higher MVA). The book defers the full quantitative analysis to Chapter 19.
questions.why_it_matters: This synthesis question is central to the entire xVA framework. Understanding the optimal collateral structure determines pricing, execution strategy, and relationship management for OTC derivatives.
common_traps: Treating IM as always beneficial or always costly without considering the full xVA balance
Ignoring FBA loss when adding IM to previously uncollateralised trades
Assuming the optimal IM level is the same for all trade types and counterparty profiles
questions.real_world_example: A bank pricing a 10-year swap with a BBB corporate: high CVA (risky counterparty) and high KVA (uncollateralised, long-dated). Adding bilateral IM significantly reduces both CVA and KVA, while the MVA is moderate for a 10-year trade. Total xVA decreases significantly. For a 1-year swap with an AA counterparty, the CVA and KVA reduction from IM is small, but MVA is high relative to trade life — net benefit of IM is negative.

questions.subtopic: Capital cost as equity return requirement
questions.question: Why must regulatory capital create a cost (KVA) even if the capital is held in risk-free assets? What is the source of the cost?
questions.answer_short: Regulatory capital is funded by equity, which requires a return (cost of capital CC, typically 10-12%). Even if the capital is held in risk-free T-bills earning 2%, shareholders require CC = 10%, creating a 8% annual cost on the committed capital.
questions.answer_long: Regulatory capital is equity — funds raised from shareholders by issuing equity. Equity investors require a return for the risk they bear (opportunity cost of capital and equity risk premium). If the bank holds $100M of regulatory capital in T-bills earning 2% annually, but shareholders require 10% return, there is an 8% annual shortfall per dollar of capital. This shortfall is the actual capital cost captured by KVA. Alternatively, the bank could deploy the capital into earning assets above risk-free, but it is constrained to hold it as safe liquid assets to meet regulatory requirements. The cost is therefore the difference between what the capital earns (risk-free or near risk-free) and what equity requires (CC).
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the source of capital cost is fundamental to KVA's rationale. Without this understanding, the formula CC × EC might seem arbitrary — understanding it as the equity return shortfall on required capital makes it concrete.
common_traps: Assuming capital cost is zero if the capital earns positive returns
Confusing the return on capital with the cost of capital (shareholders require a return, the bank delivers a return)
Ignoring that different regulatory capital requirements (CCR, CVA, market risk) all share the same equity return cost
questions.real_world_example: A bank holds $500M capital against its derivatives book. The T-bill rate is 2%, so the capital earns $10M/year. Shareholders require 10% return = $50M/year. The KVA-driven shortfall is $40M/year — a real cost to the bank that must be recovered from derivative pricing.

questions.subtopic: Rights of assessment vs default fund contributions
questions.question: Distinguish between default fund contributions and rights of assessment at a CCP, and explain why the former is typically MVA while the latter is more naturally KVA.
questions.answer_short: Default fund contributions are currently funded amounts sitting at the CCP (a cash outlay earning below-market returns) → MVA. Rights of assessment are future contingent calls not currently funded (an unfunded contingent liability requiring capital to be held) → KVA.
questions.answer_long: Default fund (DF) contributions: a clearing member posts a defined amount of cash or high-quality securities to the CCP's mutualised default fund. This is a current, funded obligation earning below-market returns — a cost analogous to IM posting. It belongs naturally in MVA. Rights of assessment: some CCPs can call for additional contributions ('rights of assessment') from clearing members in extreme scenarios beyond the initial default fund. These are not currently funded — no cash is posted today. Instead, they are contingent future obligations. These create a capital requirement (the bank must hold capital against the potential future call) rather than a current funding cost — placing them more naturally in KVA. The book notes that rights of assessment are 'unfunded and potentially heavily capitalised', justifying KVA treatment.
questions.why_it_matters: Correct classification between MVA and KVA ensures accurate xVA accounting. Misclassifying rights of assessment as MVA understates KVA and potentially understates the total cost of CCP membership.
common_traps: Treating all CCP-related costs as MVA, ignoring the KVA component for rights of assessment
Confusing default fund (funded, certain) with rights of assessment (unfunded, contingent)
Ignoring that the distinction affects the computational approach (funded cash flow vs contingent capital)
questions.real_world_example: SwapClear's standard default fund contribution is a known funded amount (MVA). Some CCPs also have rights of assessment allowing them to call for 2× the default fund from surviving members in extreme defaults. These uncalled contingent obligations require capital provisioning → KVA.

questions.question: How does the move from capital hurdle rates to explicit KVA pricing affect which types of derivatives businesses are pursued, and what transactions might a bank reduce under KVA pricing?
questions.answer_short: KVA pricing makes capital-intensive transactions explicitly more expensive, discouraging long-dated uncollateralised derivatives, high-credit-risk counterparties, and products with high add-ons. Banks will favour collateralised, shorter-dated, and lower-capital products.
questions.answer_long: Under a simple hurdle rate, all trades meeting the return threshold are equivalent. Under explicit KVA pricing, capital-intensive trades are priced higher (or become uneconomic), creating a natural incentive to: (1) Avoid long-dated uncollateralised trades (high EC profile → high KVA); (2) Avoid high-credit-risk counterparties (high default capital); (3) Favour cleared over bilateral execution (lower capital); (4) Reduce cross-currency swaps (flat capital profile → high KVA per unit time); (5) Push counterparties toward collateral agreements. This mirrors how explicit CVA pricing changed the counterparty risk landscape: banks became much more reluctant to trade uncollateralised with risky counterparties once CVA was fully priced.
questions.why_it_matters: KVA pricing has strategic implications beyond individual trade economics. It reshapes the entire derivatives business model, favouring standardised, collateralised products and potentially reducing market-making in capital-intensive segments.
common_traps: Thinking KVA only matters for xVA specialists — it affects front-office strategy
Assuming all trades become uneconomic under KVA — only the most capital-intensive ones
Ignoring competitive dynamics — if all banks price KVA, the market adjusts; if only some do, those banks lose share
questions.real_world_example: Post-2014, several major dealers significantly reduced their uncollateralised corporate derivatives business after fully implementing KVA pricing, finding that the capital costs made such trades uneconomic at market rates. Corporate clients were pushed toward clearing or collateral agreements.

questions.subtopic: Chapter 16 in the xVA framework context
questions.question: How do MVA and KVA fit into the complete xVA framework alongside CVA, DVA, FVA, and ColVA, and what unique aspect does each of Chapter 16's two components address?
questions.answer_short: CVA/DVA address credit risk; FVA/ColVA address funding and collateral costs. MVA uniquely addresses the cost of segregated IM requirements (a new post-crisis regulatory cost), while KVA uniquely addresses the cost of regulatory equity capital (previously managed via internal hurdles). Together MVA and KVA complete the post-crisis xVA suite.
questions.answer_long: The xVA framework decomposes derivative pricing into: (1) CVA: counterparty default risk (counterparty's credit risk); (2) DVA: own-default benefit; (3) FVA (FCA-FBA): funding cost/benefit of unsecured exposure; (4) ColVA: cheapest-to-deliver optionality in collateral; (5) MVA: cost of posting segregated IM, distinct from FVA which covers variation margin funding. (6) KVA: cost of regulatory equity capital, distinct from funding (FVA) which covers debt costs. MVA is the xVA for overcollateralisation (IM is more than variation margin). KVA is the xVA for regulatory equity requirements. Together, MVA and KVA capture the two major post-crisis regulatory innovations: IM mandates and capital requirements. The complete xVA suite ensures all economically relevant costs are priced into derivatives.
questions.why_it_matters: Understanding the full xVA decomposition helps practitioners ensure no cost is double-counted or omitted. MVA and KVA complete the framework started by CVA and FVA — ensuring that derivative pricing accounts for credit, funding, collateral, IM, and capital costs.
common_traps: Thinking MVA and FVA overlap completely — they address different margin components
Assuming KVA is just another form of credit adjustment — it addresses equity return requirements, not credit risk
Treating the xVA components as fully independent when overlaps (CVA/KVA, FVA/KVA) exist
questions.real_world_example: A comprehensive derivative pricing model in 2016 includes: CVA for credit risk, FVA for variation margin funding gaps, MVA for IM posting costs, KVA for regulatory capital returns, and ColVA for collateral optionality. Each component is tracked separately and managed by the xVA desk — a complete post-crisis framework.
